title: A qualitative systematic review on AI empowered self-regulated learning in higher education
extended_summary:
This paper addresses how artificial intelligence applications are being used to support self-regulated learning (SRL) in higher education, and what benefits, drawbacks, theories, and implementation patterns appear in the empirical literature. The review is motivated by growing use of AI in higher education alongside a recognized need to connect these tools to established learning theory, especially SRL frameworks.

Using a qualitative systematic review guided by PRISMA, the authors identified 14 empirical studies on AI-supported SRL in higher education. The reviewed interventions included chatbots, explainable AI dashboards and evaluation systems, automated writing evaluation tools, serious games with intelligent tutoring features, and an AI-enriched e-textbook. Across studies, these tools were used to support different SRL phases such as goal setting, progress monitoring, help-seeking, feedback, and self-evaluation.

The evidence base covered university students in higher education contexts, with most studies involving STEM or language-learning tasks and a smaller number addressing non-academic areas such as communication skills and exam anxiety. The studies were geographically diverse, including work from China, Sweden, the United States, Germany, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Ukraine, Australia, Spain, Finland, and New Zealand. Because this is a review, no single implementation setting or duration applies consistently across all included studies.

The main conclusion is that AI shows promise for supporting SRL, especially in the performance phase through real-time guidance, monitoring, feedback, and help-seeking support. However, support is often partial rather than holistic across all SRL phases, and outcomes are mixed depending on tool design, learner characteristics, and the balance between human-centered and AI-centered regulation. The review also highlights concerns about usability, feedback accuracy, inconsistent gains in self-efficacy, and the need for stronger theory-building and more rigorous empirical research on AI-supported SRL.

identified_tools.name: Chatbots — pooled
identified_tools.description: Conversational AI systems that interact with learners through dialogue to provide guidance, coaching, answers, prompts, or other instructional support.
identified_tools.use_case: Reviewed across 7 higher-education studies using chatbots for micro-learning, coaching, instructional support, reading support, and empathic feedback; comparators varied and included conventional learning methods, video-only instruction, different chatbot interaction modes, or no uniform comparison.

findings.finding_summary: The review synthesizes evidence that chatbot interventions often improved intrinsic motivation, engagement, satisfaction, or acceptance. Examples summarized in the review include higher intrinsic motivation in chatbot-based micro-learning, medium-to-high working alliance in coaching chatbots, and positive acceptance of digital self-reflection through chatbot interaction.
findings.measure: Intrinsic motivation, engagement, satisfaction, working alliance, and acceptance

findings.finding_summary: Academic performance findings for chatbots were mixed in the reviewed studies. Some chatbot-supported learning conditions improved quiz scores or learning achievement, while other studies found no significant differences from traditional methods in learning performance.
findings.measure: Course performance, quiz scores, and learning achievement

findings.finding_summary: Chatbots were synthesized as supporting self-regulated learning through goal support, immediate feedback, guidance, help-seeking, and reflection prompts, but effects on self-regulation were not uniformly positive. For example, some reviewed studies reported improved cognitive and metacognitive learning strategies, whereas another found no significant group differences in self-regulation apart from limited items.
findings.measure: Self-regulation, cognitive/metacognitive strategies, and reflective learning processes

identified_tools.name: Evaluation systems — pooled
identified_tools.description: AI-based systems that assess learner work, progress, or performance and provide automated feedback, recommendations, scores, or explanatory analytics.
identified_tools.use_case: Reviewed across 5 higher-education studies in programming and academic/language writing contexts; systems included automated writing evaluation, automated feedback systems, and explainable ML dashboards, with comparisons varying by study or examined qualitatively.

findings.finding_summary: The review indicates that evaluation/feedback systems can support self-regulated learning by helping students identify gaps, monitor progress, and engage behaviorally, cognitively, and affectively with feedback. Synthesized examples include improved SRL skills from explainable dashboards and positive use of automated feedback systems to pinpoint areas for improvement and support learner autonomy.
findings.measure: Self-regulated learning skills, progress monitoring, learner autonomy, and engagement with feedback

findings.finding_summary: In writing-focused studies, the review found that learners engaged with automated feedback in revision processes and that more active engagement tended to be associated with greater learning gains. However, outcomes depended on learner characteristics such as multilingual proficiency, digital familiarity, beliefs, and sociocultural identity, indicating heterogeneous effects.
findings.measure: Writing revision engagement and learning gains in academic writing/language learning

findings.finding_summary: For analytics-based evaluation systems in programming, the review summarizes evidence of improved learning achievement and performance when students received informative feedback and explainable recommendations. These systems were presented as helping align actions with goals and prompting further task completion.
findings.measure: Programming course achievement and performance

identified_tools.name: Serious games
identified_tools.description: AI-supported educational games that provide interactive practice, problem-solving, or instructional experiences, sometimes combined with intelligent tutoring or adaptive support.
identified_tools.use_case: Reviewed in one higher-education study of a digital logic serious game integrated with an intelligent tutoring system and reinforcement-learning support; compared against a standard lab without a game and an older game version without full personalized support.

findings.finding_summary: The review reports that the serious game with AI support was associated with higher content knowledge, quicker completion, fewer errors, and greater problem-solving efficiency. Students also reported positive attitudes toward the game and found its tools useful and easy to use.
findings.measure: Content knowledge, task completion time, errors, and problem-solving efficiency in digital systems learning

identified_tools.name: E-textbooks
identified_tools.description: Digital textbooks enhanced with AI-driven or intelligent features such as interactive supports, adaptive prompts, recommendations, or embedded learning guidance.
identified_tools.use_case: Reviewed in one higher-education introductory biology study using an AI-enriched digital textbook; examined students' cognitive load, learning strategies, self-regulation, usability, and pre/post knowledge over the course without a non-AI pooled comparator in this review.

findings.finding_summary: The review summarizes a positive learning pattern for the AI-enriched biology e-textbook, with significantly higher germane cognitive load than intrinsic or extraneous load and an observed correlation between linked suggested questions and germane load, suggesting meaningful learning. However, some students reported usability issues that negatively affected learning gains, indicating benefits were tempered by design limitations.
findings.measure: Cognitive load pattern, usability, and knowledge-related learning gains in introductory biology

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: Generative AI chatbot that produces and revises natural-language text, answers prompts, and provides writing support through conversational interaction.
identified_tools.use_case: The review mentions ChatGPT in the introduction as an example of recent large language model advances in higher education. It is also discussed in Nguyen et al. as one of the generative AI tools students were allowed to use during an academic writing task, and in Kuzminska et al. as one of the AI tools students mainly chose for team-based project work.

findings.finding_summary: In the review's summary of Nguyen et al., students who engaged in iterative, highly interactive processes with a generative AI assisting tool such as ChatGPT tended to achieve better writing performance than those using AI only as a supplementary source in a linear process.
findings.measure: writing performance

findings.finding_summary: In the review's summary of Kuzminska et al., use of AI tools mainly focused on ChatGPT and Notion AI did not improve social engagement or self-efficacy dynamics overall, though there was a positive effect for students with average self-efficacy.
findings.measure: social engagement and self-efficacy

identified_tools.name: Grammarly
identified_tools.description: AI writing assistant that checks grammar, spelling, punctuation, clarity, and style and provides revision suggestions for written text.
identified_tools.use_case: In Li & Kim, Grammarly is listed among automated feedback systems used in a personalized English language learning context. The review says it helped learners diagnose weaknesses, refine goals, monitor progress, and receive detailed feedback on language performance.

findings.finding_summary: The review reports positive perceptions and successful use of automated feedback systems including Grammarly for identifying improvement areas, monitoring progress, and boosting confidence in language learning.
findings.measure: student perceptions, use for improvement monitoring, confidence

identified_tools.name: Bashayer
identified_tools.description: A task-oriented educational chatbot embedded through WhatsApp and managed via the Freshdesk platform.
identified_tools.use_case: Al-Abdullatif et al. evaluated Bashayer with postgraduate students in Saudi higher education over 13 weeks. The chatbot supported text-based inquiry answering, access to educational consultation, and course progress summaries through WhatsApp.

findings.finding_summary: Students using the Bashayer chatbot showed higher levels of cognitive and metacognitive learning strategies than the control group.
findings.measure: MSLQ cognitive and metacognitive learning strategies

identified_tools.name: PING
identified_tools.description: A personalized instruction and need-aware gaming system based on reinforcement learning that provides adaptive support within a serious game.
identified_tools.use_case: In Hare et al., PING was integrated into the serious game Gridlock to provide personalized intelligent tutoring support for digital logic education. The review describes it as offering automated assistance, repetition, quizzes, and error diagnosis during gameplay.

findings.finding_summary: Students using the PING-enhanced game reported higher content knowledge, quicker completion times, fewer errors, and greater efficiency in problem-solving than comparison conditions.
findings.measure: content knowledge, completion time, errors, problem-solving efficiency

identified_tools.name: Gridlock
identified_tools.description: A domain-specific serious game for teaching digital logic design.
identified_tools.use_case: The review describes Gridlock in Hare et al. as a serious digital game for digital systems and computer architecture, with one version enhanced by the PING tutoring system. It supported repeated practice, quizzes, and problem-focused learning in digital logic.

findings.finding_summary: The PING-enhanced version of Gridlock was associated with higher content knowledge, faster task completion, fewer errors, and positive learner attitudes.
findings.measure: content knowledge, efficiency, learner attitudes

identified_tools.name: Pigai
identified_tools.description: A web-based automated writing evaluation system that provides scoring and feedback on English writing.
identified_tools.use_case: Pigai appears in Zhang & Xu and Zhang & Hyland as the named AWE system used in academic writing. The review says it generates real-time holistic scoring, diagnostic feedback, corrective feedback, highest and lowest scores, and overall comments, and is used for immediate feedback and revision support.

findings.finding_summary: The review reports that students engaged behaviorally, cognitively, and affectively with Pigai feedback during writing and revision, and more active engagement was associated with greater learning gains.
findings.measure: engagement with AWE feedback and learning gains

findings.finding_summary: The review reports that use of integrated feedback approaches including Pigai feedback supported improved engagement and writing performance.
findings.measure: student engagement and performance

identified_tools.name: Rasa
identified_tools.description: An open-source conversational AI framework for natural language understanding and dialogue management.
identified_tools.use_case: The review names Rasa in Mai et al. as the conversational AI used to power the writing-based interaction method in a coaching chatbot, and in Ortega-Ochoa et al. as part of the DSLab-Bot architecture for classifying and generating responses.

identified_tools.name: DSLab-Bot
identified_tools.description: A conversational agent integrated into a distributed systems learning environment to answer questions, detect emotions, and provide feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: Ortega-Ochoa et al. integrated DSLab-Bot into the syllabus and IT infrastructure for a Distributed Systems course via Mattermost. The bot responded to questions, detected emotions, and provided feedback on project execution and student responses.

findings.finding_summary: The review reports no significant differences between groups in learning performance, motivation, or self-regulation except for one item of motivation (self-efficacy) and self-regulation; however, multiple cognitive and affective chatbot feedback types were strongly correlated with metacognitive reasoning components.
findings.measure: learning performance, motivation, self-regulation, metacognitive reasoning

identified_tools.name: Mattermost
identified_tools.description: An open-source collaboration and messaging platform used here as infrastructure for chatbot integration.
identified_tools.use_case: The review mentions Mattermost as the platform within DSLab through which DSLab-Bot was integrated and made available to students in Ortega-Ochoa et al.

identified_tools.name: Freshdesk
identified_tools.description: A customer communication and ticketing platform used here to host and manage educational chatbot interactions.
identified_tools.use_case: The review states that Freshdesk hosted and managed the Bashayer chatbot, routing student WhatsApp queries, accessing a response database, and allowing teachers to manage interactions through a dashboard.

identified_tools.name: WhatsApp
identified_tools.description: A messaging application used as the communication channel for chatbot-based educational interactions.
identified_tools.use_case: In Al-Abdullatif et al., Bashayer was embedded into the learning process through WhatsApp, enabling students to interact with the chatbot over 13 weeks.

identified_tools.name: GPT-3
identified_tools.description: Large language model by OpenAI capable of natural language generation, dialogue, and text analysis, which can be used to support conversational assistance, feedback, and content creation in educational settings.
identified_tools.use_case: The review mentions GPT-3 in the description of generative AI technologies supporting writing, noting that such tools can assist with content generation, summarization, feedback, and suggestions across the writing process.

identified_tools.name: GPT-4
identified_tools.description: A large language model used for advanced text generation and language assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: The review mentions GPT-4 alongside GPT-3 as an example of generative AI technology that can support writing through content generation, summarization, feedback, and improvement suggestions.

identified_tools.name: Notion AI
identified_tools.description: An AI assistant integrated into Notion for drafting, rewriting, and idea support.
identified_tools.use_case: In Kuzminska et al., students selected their own AI tools for team-based learning projects, mainly focusing on ChatGPT and Notion AI to support project work and group dynamics.

findings.finding_summary: The review reports that AI tools mainly focused on ChatGPT and Notion AI did not improve students' social engagement or self-efficacy dynamics overall, though positive effects were seen for students with average self-efficacy.
findings.measure: social engagement and self-efficacy

identified_tools.name: ELSA
identified_tools.description: An AI-supported language learning tool used for pronunciation and spoken language feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: In Li & Kim, ELSA is listed as one of the automated feedback systems in a personalized English language learning environment. The review says it helped learners diagnose goals, monitor progress, and receive detailed feedback.

findings.finding_summary: The review reports positive perceptions and successful use of automated feedback systems including ELSA for identifying improvement areas, monitoring progress, and boosting confidence.
findings.measure: student perceptions, monitoring progress, confidence

identified_tools.name: PaperRater
identified_tools.description: An automated writing evaluation and proofreading tool that provides language feedback and scoring.
identified_tools.use_case: In Li & Kim, PaperRater is named among the automated feedback systems students used for goal setting, diagnostic insight, and detailed language feedback in personalized English learning.

findings.finding_summary: The review reports positive perceptions and successful use of automated feedback systems including PaperRater for identifying areas for improvement and supporting confidence and learner autonomy.
findings.measure: student perceptions, diagnostic use, confidence

identified_tools.name: MaiMemo
identified_tools.description: A learning support tool used to track language learning progress.
identified_tools.use_case: In Li & Kim, MaiMemo is mentioned as one of the tools used to track learner progress and support motivation in a personalized English learning ecology.

findings.finding_summary: The review indicates that tools such as MaiMemo supported progress tracking and motivation within students' automated feedback system use.
findings.measure: progress tracking and motivation

identified_tools.name: Speech Rate Meter
identified_tools.description: A speech analysis tool used to assess speaking rate as part of language learning feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: In Li & Kim, Speech Rate Meter is named as a tool used to measure the gap between learners' current abilities and their target language goals.

findings.finding_summary: The review says tools such as Speech Rate Meter were used to help learners judge discrepancies between current performance and goals in language learning.
findings.measure: gap analysis between current ability and goals

identified_tools.name: VoiceAnalyst
identified_tools.description: A voice analysis application used to assess speech-related performance.
identified_tools.use_case: In Li & Kim, VoiceAnalyst is mentioned among tools used to measure gaps between learners' current abilities and desired language goals.

findings.finding_summary: The review reports that tools such as VoiceAnalyst supported self-judgment by helping learners assess the gap between their current abilities and target goals.
findings.measure: self-judgment of current ability versus goals

identified_tools.name: Google Scholar
identified_tools.description: A scholarly search engine used to locate academic literature and sources.
identified_tools.use_case: The review mentions Google Scholar in Nguyen et al. as one of the tools participants were allowed to use during the academic writing task alongside ChatGPT and other tools.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review using PRISMA procedures to synthesize 14 empirical studies, which places it above single-study observational work. However, it is a qualitative systematic review rather than a meta-analysis, and the included studies are methodologically heterogeneous, so there are some credibility concerns relative to the highest tier.
impact_tier_rationale: The review reports generally promising but mixed evidence, with benefits concentrated in some SRL phases and some studies showing null or inconsistent effects. Because no pooled effect size is provided and impacts are heterogeneous and often unclear, the overall impact is best classified as modest or unclear.
